area: Area IV. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can plan and fly a power-off 180° approach from the downwind key position, manage your glide with path, flaps and slips, and touch down on or within 200 feet beyond a chosen point, or go around safely when it will not work.
why: The real skill is judging how far your airplane will glide with the engine at idle. That is the same judgment you need to reach a field after an engine failure [[24:195|AFH 9-24]] [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

prereading.what: Power-off accuracy approaches: gliding distance, key positions, the 90° and 180° approaches, common errors.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 9, 9-24 to 9-27

prereading.what: Glide ratio, best glide speed, effect of weight and wind on the glide, gliding turns, stretching the glide.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 3, 3-21 to 3-24

prereading.what: Use of flaps, base leg placement, aiming point, runway shape, stabilized approach and go-around limits.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 9, 9-1 to 9-6

prereading.what: Go-arounds, intentional slips and their limits, crosswind approach and touchdown.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 9, 9-10 to 9-18

prereading.what: Energy management: altitude and airspeed as total energy; the roles of throttle and elevator.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 4, 4-1 to 4-4

prereading.what: Simulated emergency landings, high and low final approaches, floating during the round out.
prereading.label: AFH Ch 9, 9-28 to 9-32

warmup: You close the throttle abeam your chosen spot at 1,000 feet AGL. Without touching the throttle again, what are all the ways you could still change where you touch down? Which of them would you never use?

key_terms.def: Gliding with the engine idling, in a set pattern, to touch down on a given point or within a set distance beyond it [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
The point on downwind, abreast of the landing spot, where you close the throttle in a 180° approach [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].
The 45° key position on base: the landing spot appears at a 45° angle from the nose [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
The speed that gives the most forward distance for each foot of altitude lost in still air; it occurs at maximum L/D [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].
Distance traveled compared with altitude lost. 10,000 feet forward for 1,000 feet down is 10 to 1 [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].
A speed a little slower than best glide that keeps you aloft longest, but covers less distance [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
A stabilized, power-off descent at best glide speed [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Pulling the nose up to try to glide farther. It slows you below best glide, shortens the glide and can stall you [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Angling the base leg away from or toward the runway when conditions are not as expected [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].
Planning, watching and controlling altitude and airspeed as the airplane's total energy [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].
Stalling speed in the landing configuration; base and final targets are often 1.4 VSO and 1.3 VSO [[24:173|AFH 9-2]] [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

body.p: In a power-off accuracy approach you glide with the engine idling, in a set pattern, to touch down on a chosen point or within a set distance beyond it. The goal is the judgment and procedures to fly the airplane, without power, to a safe landing [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
The real basis of the maneuver is your ability to estimate how far the airplane will glide. The distance to cover sets how much maneuvering you need from a given altitude [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

Exact height in feet matters less than knowing your normal glide angle. A pilot who knows it can predict, quite well, the spot along a ground path where the airplane will land. That is what lets you choose a field in a real emergency [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

head: Normal approach
Power-off accuracy approach
rows: Pitch and power are used together for descent angle and airspeed [[24:175|AFH 9-4]]
Airspeed, and that also changes the glide angle [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]
Normally the first third of the runway [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]
A chosen point; ACS: on it or within 200 feet beyond (ACS CA.IV.M.S8)
Pattern shape, flaps, slips, speed [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]; never the throttle [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]

callout.text: Spot landings matter, but a safe, well-flown approach and landing matter more. Never give up a good landing just to hit the spot [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

Flying a single-engine turboprop that sinks too fast at flight idle? Don't feather the prop in training. Set enough power to match the performance you would get with the prop feathered [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

check.q: What is the real basis of every power-off accuracy approach?
check.a: The ability to estimate the distance the airplane glides to a landing [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

chunks.title: Best glide speed and the normal glide

body.p: Best glide speed gives the greatest forward distance for a given loss of altitude in still air. It happens at the highest lift-to-drag ratio (L/D). Faster or slower than that, drag goes up and the glide ratio gets worse [[24:83|AFH 3-22]].
Weight does not change the glide angle if you fly the right speed. A heavier airplane must glide faster to get the same glide ratio. It covers the same distance, just in less time [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
Drag items like flaps, gear and cowl flaps steepen the glide. To hold airspeed with more drag you must lower the nose, and the glide path gets steeper and shorter [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

head: Where you are
Pitch down
Pitch up
rows: Less speed, much steeper descent angle

body.p: That table comes straight from the AFH [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. If you are too fast, raise the nose. If you are too slow, lower it. Raise the pitch too high and the airplane settles fast from low speed and too little lift [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

To enter the glide, close the throttle (prop forward if you have one) and hold altitude with back pressure until the speed bleeds to best glide. Then set the pitch for that speed and trim [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. With no slipstream, expect to need slight left rudder to stay coordinated [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

callout.text: Sound, sight and feel: rising wind noise means rising speed. Use all three airspeed cues, not just the needle [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

check.q: Two airplanes with the same L/D glide from the same height. One is heavier. Which glides farther?
check.a: Neither. Both cover the same distance; the heavier one flies faster and gets there sooner [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

chunks.title: Energy management with the throttle closed

body.p: Your total energy is altitude (potential energy) plus airspeed (kinetic energy) [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. Normally the throttle is the total energy control and the elevator trades energy between altitude and speed [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].

In this maneuver the throttle is fixed at idle [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. So you cannot add energy. You can only spend what you have wisely. High lift and drag devices can only increase drag [[24:90|AFH 4-4]], so with the throttle closed they can only take energy away.

Read your energy state with the matrix. Higher and faster or lower and slower is a total energy error. Higher and slower or lower and faster is a distribution error that the elevator can fix. Normally a total energy error is fixed with the throttle [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]. In this maneuver the throttle stays closed, so you need the AFH glide tools instead.

head: Energy state, throttle closed (application)
AFH tools that fit
rows: Too much energy (high, or on path but fast)
Dog-leg away from the runway on base, S-turns, earlier flaps [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]; flaps or a brief forward slip on final [[24:197|AFH 9-26]] [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]
Dog-leg toward the runway on base, later flaps [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]; delay full flaps until you know you will make the point [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]
Never stretch the glide or retract the flaps [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]. If in doubt about the approach, go around [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]

body.p: Starting with the same energy (airspeed and height) every time you close the throttle makes the maneuver predictable [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. Application: fly the same altitude, distance and speed at the key every lap, so the wind is the main thing left to judge.

callout.text: Energy mistakes are a factor in loss of control in flight, CFIT and approach-and-landing accidents, the three most common fatal accident types [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

check.q: With the throttle at idle, why can flaps and slips only help when you are high?
check.a: They add drag, and drag can only remove energy; they cannot add it back [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].

chunks.title: Wind: how it moves your landing spot

body.p: Wind changes gliding distance over the ground. A tailwind makes you glide farther because of the higher groundspeed. A headwind makes you glide less far [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
In a 180° approach the wind acts on every leg. Final is normally flown into the wind, so there is usually a crosswind on base [[24:173|AFH 9-2]], and the downwind leg has a tailwind.

bullets: Downwind: a tailwind can stretch the downwind leg too far. That is a listed common error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].
Base: place the base leg for the wind. Stronger wind on final means a base closer to the runway for a steeper glide on final (Figure 9-25) [[24:196|AFH 9-25]] [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
Base: the crab you need to hold your track tells you the wind's strength and direction. Use it to plan the turn to final and when to lower flaps [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
Final: in a headwind you may glide slightly above best glide to stabilize the rest of the approach [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].
Not correcting for drift on base is another listed common error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

body.p: Wind also matters on the ground. A 10-knot tailwind adds about 21 percent to landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

At a high density altitude you land at the same indicated airspeed as at sea level, but the true airspeed is higher. At 5,000 feet the minimum landing distance is about 16 percent longer than at sea level [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

callout.text: Learn to read the wind from the windsock, smoke, dust or water. In a real engine failure, nobody gives you an ATIS [[24:199|AFH 9-28]].

check.q: The wind on final is strong today. Where should you place the base leg?
check.a: Closer to the runway than normal, for a steeper glide on final [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

chunks.title: The 90° approach: base key to touchdown

body.p: The 180° approach ends with a 90° approach, so learn that part first. The glide from the base key through the turn to final is the last part of every accuracy landing [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

bullets: Turn base with a medium bank, reduce power slightly, and slow to normal base-leg speed. Hold speed, drift correction and altitude to the 45° key position [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

At the 45° key the spot appears at 45° from the nose. Close the throttle fully, prop to full increase rpm, and hold altitude until you reach the recommended glide speed, or 1.4 VSO if none is published [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
Lower the nose to hold glide speed and trim. Lower flaps gradually and adjust pitch for the right descent angle [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
Plan the base-to-final turn so you roll out on the centerline [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
On final, add flaps as needed and set 1.3 VSO, then trim [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

callout.text: Plan slightly high. If you are slightly high in your current configuration, you are sure to make the aiming point, and drag can take care of the rest [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

body.p: Delay full flaps until you are sure adding them will not make you land short [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]. On short final, put your full attention on a good, safe landing, not the spot. Late changes to approach angle and speed are not appropriate [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

check.q: What speed do you hold at the 45° key if the POH gives no glide speed?
check.a: 1.4 VSO, held by keeping altitude until the speed decays to it, then lowering the nose [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

chunks.title: The 180° approach: downwind key and the turn

body.p: In the 180° approach you glide with idle power from the downwind leg to the preselected spot. You fly a 90° turn without power to reach the base key at the right height for a 90° approach. It takes more planning and judgment than the 90° approach [[24:197|AFH 9-26]] [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

head: Step
What the AFH says
rows: Fly a downwind heading parallel to the runway. Start no higher than about 1,000 feet AGL, except in large airplanes [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]
Same distance from the runway as a normal pattern [[24:196|AFH 9-25]], about 1/2 to 1 mile [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]
Abreast of the spot: close the throttle, hold altitude while slowing to glide speed or 1.4 VSO [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]
A uniform turn with a medium or slightly steeper bank. Bank and amount of turn depend on the glide angle and the wind [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]
Place it to save or lose altitude so you reach the spot; flaps may come out before the base key if needed [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]
Fly it exactly like the 90° approach [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]

body.p: The base key is a judgment point, not a fixed landmark. Pilots who tie it to a tree or a crossroad are lost when that object isn't there. Vary the altitude and location in practice [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].
Judge height by sight up to about 1,000 feet with fair accuracy. Above that, ground features merge and you need the altimeter to help [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

callout.text: A downwind leg flown too far from the runway is the first common error on the AFH list. Too far out and you can't glide back [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

check.q: Where exactly is the downwind key position?
check.a: On downwind, abreast of (opposite) the landing spot, where you close the throttle [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

chunks.title: Shaping the glide: flaps, slips, S-turns and dog-legs

body.p: Square patterns show good planning, but they are not required. When things are not as expected, you may dog-leg away from or toward the runway on base. You may also use S-turns, slips, early or late flaps, or a speed a little off best glide to reach the aiming point and touch down where planned [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

Flaps add lift and drag and steepen the descent; they help set both the landing spot and the descent angle [[24:172|AFH 9-1]]. Up to about 15° mostly adds lift; beyond 15° adds a lot of drag. Add them in steps so pitch changes stay small, and re-trim [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

head: Tool
Use it when
Watch out
rows: High: lower them as required [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]; initial flaps may come out before the base key [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]
Too early is a common error; full flaps only when you know you'll make it [[24:198|AFH 9-27]] [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]
High: steepen the descent briefly without gaining speed [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]
Check POH slip limits, especially with flaps down [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
When high: a listed tool [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]; the longer path uses up height (application)
Keep them coordinated and away from other traffic
When conditions are not as expected [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. Application: away if high, toward the runway if low
Never to fix a low approach [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]
Sudden loss of lift and a higher sink rate [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]

body.p: Slip hazards (ACS R7): some airplanes limit slips by time or fuel quantity, because uncoordinated flight can push fuel to one side of a tank and starve the engine. There may also be limits on slips with flaps for aerodynamic reasons [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Flaps change the downwash on the horizontal tail and the tail-down force [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

In a slip your airspeed indicator may read wrong because of where the pitot tube and static vents are. Judge the slip by attitude, sound and control feel. Control airspeed with the elevator [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

callout.text: The AFM/POH wins. Its configurations, speeds and limits come first whenever they differ from the AFH [[24:172|AFH 9-1]].

check.q: You are low on base with partial flaps out. Should you raise them to stretch the glide?
check.a: No. Never retract flaps to reach the spot; it causes a sudden loss of lift and more sink [[24:197|AFH 9-26]] [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

body.p: Brief first: the POH glide speed (or 1.4 VSO), flap limits and slip limits, the wind, and which point the examiner wants [[24:172|AFH 9-1]] [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

bullets: 1. Enter downwind at pattern altitude, no higher than about 1,000 feet AGL, at normal pattern distance [[24:198|AFH 9-27]] [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].
2. Finish the before-landing checklist on downwind, including the gear in a retractable [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].
3. Radio, non-towered: "On left/right downwind for runway XX." At a towered field, follow ATC [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].
4. Confirm the touchdown point and crab as needed to fly parallel to the runway (ACS CA.IV.M.S4, S5).
5. Abreast of the point: throttle closed, prop forward, hold altitude until glide speed, then pitch for it and trim [[24:198|AFH 9-27]] [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].
6. Turn base with a uniform medium or slightly steeper bank, sized for the wind and your glide [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]. Call "On left/right base" [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].
7. On base: read your crab for the wind, judge the angle to the spot, and shape the base (dog-leg) to save or lose height. Initial flaps if needed [[24:197|AFH 9-26]] [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].
8. Coordinated turn to final, rolling out on centerline. Call "On final" [[24:197|AFH 9-26]] [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].
9. On final: flaps as needed, 1.3 VSO, trim. Slip briefly if high. Full flaps only when you know you'll make it [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
10. Keep the engine warm and cleared as your POH and CFI direct [[24:200|AFH 9-29]], but never use the throttle to extend the glide [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].
11. Round out and touch down on the main gear at or just above stall speed, in the proper landing attitude [[24:180|AFH 9-9]]. ACS: on the point or within 200 feet beyond it (ACS CA.IV.M.S8).
12. After landing, clear the runway and complete the after-landing checklist [[24:181|AFH 9-10]].

callout.text: Throttle use after the downwind key does more than break the maneuver. Using it to increase the glide is a listed common error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]. Clearing the engine is fine; stretching with it is not.
Keep one hand on the throttle throughout the approach and landing, so you can add power at once if a hazard appears [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].

check.q: When do you close the throttle in a power-off 180° approach, and what do you do next?
check.a: Abreast of the spot on downwind (the downwind key). Hold altitude until you slow to glide speed or 1.4 VSO, then pitch for it and trim [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

chunks.title: Crosswind: crab on base, sideslip to touchdown

body.p: On base, crab into the wind to keep your ground track square to the runway [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. On final, a crab or a sideslip can hold the path, and a forward slip can steepen the glide [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

If you forward slip in a crosswind, lower the upwind wing so you bank into the wind. That makes it easier to stay on the path [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Slipping the same way the wind blows is a common error [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

bullets: Before the round out, change to a sideslip (wing low): rudder lines the nose up with the runway, aileron gives just enough bank to stop the drift [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].
Keep the upwind wing down through the round out. Add more rudder and aileron as you slow [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
Touch down on the upwind main wheel first [[24:188|AFH 9-17]]. ACS: no side drift, longitudinal axis aligned with and over the centerline (ACS CA.IV.M.S8).
Rollout: aileron into the wind, full into the wind as you stop [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

callout.text: Touching down in a drift side-loads the gear. As little as 10° of cornering angle makes a side load of half the supported weight and can roll over a tricycle-gear airplane [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].
If full opposite rudder can't stop the turn at the bank you need, the crosswind is too strong for that runway. Use another runway or airport [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

check.q: Right crosswind on final and you are high. Which wing goes down in the forward slip?
check.a: The right (upwind) wing, so you slip into the wind [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

chunks.title: Choosing the runway, the path and the spot

body.p: Choose the runway, path and touchdown point by your skill, the airplane's performance and limits, the distance available and the wind (ACS CA.IV.M.R1). The touchdown point must leave room to stop.
Picking the runway numbers as your touchdown point leaves no cushion for a mechanical problem or a misjudgment. A point farther down the runway gives you a safety margin [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

head: Effect (ACS R2) or factor
Why it matters
rows: Drift on base and final. Slip into the wind and touch down with no drift [[24:197|AFH 9-26]] [[24:187|AFH 9-16]]. If full opposite rudder can't hold it, use another runway [[24:188|AFH 9-17]]
A headwind that turns into a tailwind cuts airspeed; a microburst on approach can force you to the ground short of the runway [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]
Stretches the downwind leg [[24:198|AFH 9-27]] and adds about 21 percent landing distance for 10 knots [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]
Behind a larger airplane, stay at or above its path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]
Can cause hydroplaning: poor steering and braking [[24:208|AFH 9-37]]
Plan the path and the point around them (ACS CA.IV.M.S3, S4)
Floating can carry you well past the point with too little runway left [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]
Each 10 feet above 50 feet adds about 200 feet of landing distance [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]]

body.p: LAHSO: you may be offered a land and hold short clearance. The PIC can accept or decline it, and should decline if it would compromise safety. Plan for it before the flight: find out if the airport has LAHSO, know the available landing distance (ALD), and know which LAHSO runways work for your airplane's landing distance [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].

callout.text: A power-off approach can't be fixed with power once you are low. If the hold-short point leaves no margin for a float past your spot, decline LAHSO [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].

check.q: Why does the AFH advise against picking the runway numbers as your touchdown point?
check.a: It gives no safety cushion for a mechanical problem or misjudgment; a point farther down adds margin [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

chunks.title: Go around or land: the decision

body.p: A go-around is a normal maneuver, not a failure. Reasons include ATC, a hazard on the runway, overtaking traffic, wind shear, wake turbulence or an unstable approach [[24:181|AFH 9-10]]. Plan for one every time: any approach or landing may end in a go-around. Two things delay it: landing expectancy and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

The ACS is blunt about this Task. Going around because you can't meet the tolerances is unsatisfactory. A go-around for runway safety issues beyond your control is not. And neither you nor the examiner may force a landing to finish the Task (ACS Appendix 3).

bullets: Stabilized approach limits still apply: go around if not stabilized by 500 feet above airport elevation in VMC, and right away if it becomes unstable below 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
A sink rate above 800 to 1,000 fpm is excessive; go around if it gets there [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].
Too slow and too low: go around [[24:202|AFH 9-31]].
Floating long past the spot with runway running out: go around rather than force it on [[24:203|AFH 9-32]] [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

body.p: Wind shear can turn a headwind into a tailwind and cut your airspeed. On approach, a microburst can force an airplane to the ground short of the runway [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. With no power in hand, that leaves very little margin. Go around early.
Go-around: power first (full, smooth, carb heat off if applicable), then attitude (forward pressure for the nose-up trim, right rudder), then configuration (flaps up in steps) [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

callout.text: It is always better to make a good landing away from the spot than a poor landing on it [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

check.q: You will clearly land 300 feet short of the spot unless you add power. What now?
check.a: Go around. Don't stretch the glide [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]. The ACS counts that go-around as not meeting the Task, but forcing a bad approach is never acceptable (ACS Appendix 3).

chunks.title: Low and slow in the pattern: stall, spin, traffic, wake

body.p: Gliding turns need more back pressure than straight glides, but less rudder than you expect without power. Too much rudder in a gliding turn, plus opposite aileron and back pressure, sets up a cross-control condition. A stall there almost certainly means a rapid, unrecoverable spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]].

Skidding turns to stretch the glide are a listed common error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]. A skidding cross-control stall is most likely in a base-to-final turn after an overshoot. Keep bank at or below 30° there and go around instead of skidding [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

Stretching the glide with back pressure is the cardinal sin. It slows you below best glide, makes you land short, and can stall you [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Flying too low over the approach area also brings terrain and obstacles close (ACS CA.IV.M.R5).

head: Hazard
What to do
rows: Most midairs happen in good weather, by day, within 5 miles of an airport [[24:31|AFH 1-10]]. Make position calls and keep looking [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].
Before turning final, make sure no one is already on final. Don't cut in or rush the turn; go around [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].
Others may not expect it. Communicate your position in the pattern on the CTAF [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].
Landing behind a larger airplane: stay at or above its path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

body.p: Distractions: the point, the wind, the examiner and the radio all compete for your attention. Many distractions start as a minor problem. When overloaded: stop, think, slow down, prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

callout.text: Fixating on the spot is the classic loss of situational awareness in this maneuver. On short final the landing comes first, not the spot [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

check.q: You are short on base and tempted to skid the turn to final to save altitude. Why not?
check.a: Skidding turns to stretch the glide are a common error and set up a cross-control stall that can become a spin [[24:198|AFH 9-27]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

head: What the examiner checks
Standard
rows: On the specified point or within 200 feet beyond it; short of the point is out (ACS CA.IV.M.S8)
Proper pitch attitude, no side drift, longitudinal axis aligned with and over the centerline (ACS CA.IV.M.S8)
As necessary, slip into the crosswind, then change to a sideslip before touchdown (ACS CA.IV.M.S7)
Downwind parallel to the runway; a flightpath planned for altitude, wind, terrain and obstructions (ACS CA.IV.M.S3, S5)
One caused by missing the tolerances is unsatisfactory; never force the landing (ACS Appendix 3)

body.p: Common errors in power-off accuracy approaches [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]:

bullets: Downwind leg too far from the runway.
Downwind leg stretched too long by a tailwind.
Not correcting for drift on base.
Skidding turns to try to glide farther.
Forgetting the landing gear in a retractable.
Trying to stretch the glide when undershooting.
Flaps or gear out too early.
Using the throttle to extend the glide instead of just clearing the engine.
Forcing the airplane onto the runway to avoid overshooting the spot.

callout.text: Commercial standard: the private forward slip to a landing allows up to 400 feet beyond the point (ACS PA.IV.M.S8); here you get only 200 feet (ACS CA.IV.M.S8). Practice until you can say, from the base key, whether you will land short, on or long.

check.q: You touch down 20 feet before the painted point, smoothly and on centerline. Does it meet the ACS?
check.a: No. The standard is on the point or within 200 feet beyond it (ACS CA.IV.M.S8).

f1.caption: Figure 9-27. 180° power-off approach.
f1.alt: An airplane flies downwind past a runway, closes the throttle at the downwind leg key position abreast of a yellow landing spot (a 90° marker shows the spot square to the downwind leg), turns base with a medium or steeper bank, reaches the key position and lowers partial flaps at 1.4 VSO, then turns final and lowers full flaps as needed at 1.3 VSO.

f2.caption: Figure 9-26. 90° power-off approach.
f2.alt: An airplane on base leg at reduced power reaches the base key position, where a yellow dashed line to the runway spot makes a 45° angle; it closes the throttle at 1.4 VSO, lowers partial flaps, turns final and lowers full flaps as needed at 1.3 VSO.

f3.caption: Figure 9-25. Plan the base leg for wind conditions.
f3.alt: Three base legs to runway 36: red for strong wind is closest to the runway for a steeper final, orange for medium wind is closer, and blue for light wind is a normal base for a normal final.

f4.caption: Figure 3-24. Best glide speed provides the greatest forward distance.
f4.alt: An airplane gliding toward a runway; the yellow best glide speed path reaches the runway, while red too fast and too slow paths both hit the ground short of it.

f5.caption: Figure 9-1. Effect of flaps on the landing point.
f5.alt: Three glide paths from the same point at constant airspeed and power: full flaps touches down earliest on the runway, half flaps farther along, and no flaps farthest down the runway.

f6.caption: Figure 4-11. An energy state matrix that translates the main altitude-speed deviations into energy errors relative to the desired energy state (5).
f6.alt: Three-by-three color table: rows higher, desired and lower altitude; columns slower, desired and faster airspeed; each box shows total, potential and kinetic energy as low, OK or high, with box 5 the desired state.

scenario.title: Checkride day: gusty wind and a busy pattern
scenario.setup: Your examiner asks for a power-off 180° to the 1,000-foot markers on runway 27 at a non-towered field. Wind is 300° at 14 knots, gusting. You are at 1,000 feet AGL on a left downwind. A larger twin landed on runway 27 two minutes ago, and a Cessna calls a 4-mile straight-in final for 27 just as you reach the key.

questions.q: Your downwind has a tailwind. What common error is waiting for you, and how do you avoid it?
questions.a: Letting the tailwind stretch the downwind leg too far [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]. Close the throttle right at the abeam point, keep normal pattern distance, and turn base promptly [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

questions.q: With a stiff wind on final, where do you put the base leg?
questions.a: Closer to the runway than normal, for a steeper glide on final [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. Your crab on base confirms how strong the wind is [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

questions.q: The Cessna on the straight-in will arrive about when you do. What do you do?
questions.a: Announce your position on the CTAF and keep looking [[17:8|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]]. Make sure no one is already on final before you turn, and don't cut in or rush the turn; go around if there is a conflict [[24:168|AFH 8-4]].

questions.q: Where should you touch down relative to the twin's landing?
questions.a: Stay at or above its approach path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. If that conflicts with your spot, safety wins over the spot [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

questions.q: You are high on final with full flaps. Can you slip?
questions.a: Only if the POH allows it. Some airplanes limit slips with flaps for aerodynamic reasons, or limit slip time and fuel quantity [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Slip into the wind (right wing low here) [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

questions.q: At 200 feet a gust drops your airspeed sharply and you sink below the path. What now?
questions.a: That may be wind shear [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Go around: power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Never stretch the glide with back pressure [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. A safety go-around beats forcing the landing (ACS Appendix 3).

skills.do: Complete the before-landing checklist on downwind, before the key, and the after-landing checklist once clear.
skills.practice: Finish the checklist, including gear, before you reach the abeam point every time [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

skills.do: Make downwind, base and final calls on the CTAF, or follow ATC at a towered field.
skills.practice: Chair-fly the three calls with the runway number [[17:9|AC 90-66C 9.11.2]].

skills.do: Plan and fly a path from the downwind key to the point, allowing for altitude, wind, terrain and obstructions.
skills.practice: Shape the base leg for the wind and practice dog-legs and S-turns to fix high or low [[24:196|AFH 9-25]] [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

skills.do: Pick (or accept) the touchdown point that suits the wind, surface, obstacles and airplane.
skills.practice: Choose a point beyond the numbers for margin, and vary it each lap [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

skills.do: Fly downwind parallel to the runway at normal pattern distance, no higher than about 1,000 feet AGL.
skills.practice: Crab for wind to hold a parallel track; don't drift out [[24:198|AFH 9-27]] [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].

skills.do: Configure correctly: throttle closed at the key, glide speed or 1.4 VSO, flaps in steps, 1.3 VSO on final, per the POH.
skills.practice: Call out each configuration change and its speed; delay full flaps until the spot is assured [[24:197|AFH 9-26]] [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

skills.do: In a crosswind, slip into the wind and change to a sideslip before touchdown.
skills.practice: On a long final, practice the forward-slip to sideslip change before the round out [[24:184|AFH 9-13]] [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].

skills.do: Touch down at proper pitch, on or within 200 feet beyond the point, no drift, aligned with and over the centerline.
skills.practice: Have your CFI note where you touch down each time. Hold the proper landing attitude; never force it on to hit the spot [[24:180|AFH 9-9]] [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

quiz.q: In a power-off accuracy approach, what does pitch control?
options: Airspeed, which also changes the glide angle
Altitude only
Engine rpm
Nothing; trim does it all
quiz.why: Power is fixed at idle, so pitch is adjusted to control airspeed, and that also changes the glide or descent angle [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

quiz.q: You are slower than best glide speed. What happens if you raise the nose?
options: You glide farther because the nose-up pitch stretches the glide
Nothing changes because power is idle and the glide angle stays the same
Airspeed rises as the nose comes up and the wing makes more lift
Airspeed drops and the descent angle gets much steeper
quiz.why: Below best glide, pitching up reduces airspeed and will greatly steepen the descent angle [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

quiz.q: Where is the downwind key position in a 180° power-off approach?
options: Abeam the approach end of the runway
Where you turn base
Abreast of the desired landing spot
At the 45° point on base
quiz.why: When abreast of or opposite the landing spot, close the throttle. That point is the downwind key position [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH say about the starting altitude for a 180° power-off approach in a light airplane?
options: Usually not above 1,000 feet AGL
Exactly 800 feet AGL
Any altitude the pilot chooses
At least 1,500 feet AGL
quiz.why: The starting altitude varies by airplane but should usually not exceed 1,000 feet AGL, except with large airplanes [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

quiz.q: A tailwind on downwind most often leads to which error?
options: A base leg too close to the runway
An overextended downwind leg
Too slow a glide
Too early a turn to final
quiz.why: Overextension of the downwind leg from a tailwind is a listed common error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

quiz.q: When should you lower full flaps on final in this maneuver?
options: At the downwind key, so the airplane is set up early
Only when it's clear they won't make you land short
As soon as you turn base, so the flaps are set early
Never; it is a no-flap maneuver, so flaps are not used
quiz.why: Full flaps should be delayed until it is clear that adding them will not cause the landing to be short of the point [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

quiz.q: Which of these does the AFH list as a way to fix a misjudged power-off approach?
options: Adding a small burst of power on base to fix the path
Raising flaps to stretch the glide when landing short
Dog-legging the base leg away from or toward the runway
Pulling the nose up to glide farther as the spot rises
quiz.why: Pilots may dog-leg away from or toward the runway on base, and use S-turns, slips and flap timing [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. Raising flaps or stretching are never acceptable [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

quiz.q: Which runway condition can cause hydroplaning on your power-off landing?
options: A dry runway with a slight upslope
Standing water, slush, or wet snow
A dry grass strip
A dry runway with a tailwind
quiz.why: Hydroplaning can happen on a runway contaminated with standing water, slush, or wet snow, and it hurts steering and braking [[24:208|AFH 9-37]]. Slope, grass and tailwind change landing distance but are not hydroplaning causes [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

quiz.q: Why might you not trust the airspeed indicator during a forward slip?
options: Flaps block the pitot tube whenever they are extended during a slip
The engine is at idle, so the indicator reads low until power is added
The gyros tumble in a slip, which also corrupts the airspeed indication
Pitot and static locations can cause large errors in a slip
quiz.why: Because of the pitot tube and static vent location, some airspeed indicators have considerable error in a slip [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH, what two things most often delay a needed go-around?
options: Fuel state and weather
ATC delays and traffic
Landing expectancy and pride
Flap setting and trim
quiz.why: Delay in starting a go-around normally comes from landing expectancy (believing the approach is sure to work) and pride (seeing a go-around as failure) [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

takeaways: The whole maneuver is judging glide distance; know your normal glide angle [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].
Close the throttle abreast of the spot and hold altitude to glide speed or 1.4 VSO [[24:198|AFH 9-27]], then lower the nose and trim [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
Plan slightly high; fix high with path and drag, fix low with a shorter path and later flaps [[24:196|AFH 9-25]] [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
Never stretch the glide, retract flaps or use the throttle to reach the spot [[24:197|AFH 9-26]] [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].
Touch down on the point or within 200 feet beyond it, aligned and without drift (ACS CA.IV.M.S8).
A good landing off the spot beats a poor one on it; go around rather than force it [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
cfi_notes: Teach the 90° approach from the base key first, then add the downwind segment; the AFH builds the 180° on top of the 90° [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].
Vary the pattern altitude and position on practice laps so students don't anchor the base key to a landmark [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

Application: tie the maneuver to energy. With the throttle closed nothing can add energy, and drag devices can only take it away [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]; the AFH tools (base placement, S-turns, slips, flap timing) only change how the energy you have is spent [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

The AFH stabilized approach list includes a power setting not below the AFM minimum for approach, and says to focus on the elements rather than insist on every criterion [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. The power-off accuracy approach fixes power at idle [[24:195|AFH 9-24]], and the AFH does not reconcile the two. Teach the other elements (path, speed, configuration, sink rate) and the 300-foot go-around rule, and check the AFM/POH for any idle-power note.
Make clear who controls the throttle; many near accidents in simulated power-off work came from confusion over it [[24:200|AFH 9-29]].
Examiners often probe the ACS go-around note: a go-around for missing the tolerances is unsatisfactory, but forcing the landing is never acceptable (ACS Appendix 3).
Watch for skidding turns and attempts to stretch the glide when students run short; both are on the AFH common error list [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].
gaps: Airplane-specific best glide speed, flap limits, slip limits and approach speeds come from the POH/AFM, which is not in the sources.

Tail stalls with flaps in a slip (CA.IV.M.R7): the sources only say flaps change tail downwash and tail-down force and that slips with flaps may be limited for aerodynamic reasons; no detailed mechanism is given.
The sources give no method to calculate a glide in wind (groundspeed-based glide distance) beyond the statement that tailwinds lengthen and headwinds shorten it.
No source gives a specific procedure for LAHSO or wake avoidance during a power-off approach; guidance is taken from the general AIM text.

activities.title: Glide speed cause and effect
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then tap what it does to your glide.

pairs.r: Most forward distance for the altitude lost in still air
More drag and a worse glide ratio

pairs.l: Pulling the nose up to stretch
pairs.r: Slower than best glide; you land short or stall

pairs.l: Adding flaps or gear in the glide
pairs.r: Lower nose to hold speed; steeper, shorter glide
Longest time aloft but less distance covered

activities.title: High or low: pick the right fix
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Dog-leg away from the runway on base
Dog-leg toward the runway on base
Place the base leg closer to the runway

activities.title: True or false: wind and the glide
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: A tailwind makes the airplane glide farther over the ground.
cards.why: Yes. With a tailwind the airplane glides farther because of the higher groundspeed [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

cards.s: In a strong wind on final, you should place the base leg farther from the runway than normal.
cards.why: No. Strong wind calls for the closest base, for a steeper glide on final [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

cards.s: Wind shear that turns a headwind into a tailwind lowers your airspeed.
cards.why: Yes. A headwind changing to a tailwind causes a decrease in airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

cards.s: When final is flown into the wind, there is usually a crosswind on the base leg.
cards.why: Yes. Final is normally into the wind, so base usually has a crosswind; hold a drift correction on base [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

cards.s: A 10-knot tailwind adds only about 5 percent to landing distance.
cards.why: No. A 10-knot tailwind increases landing distance by about 21 percent [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

cards.s: At a high-elevation field you land at a higher indicated airspeed than at sea level.
cards.why: No. You land at the same IAS, but the TAS is higher, so the landing is longer [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

activities.title: Name the parts of the 180°
activities.intro: Drag each name to its numbered pin.

activities.title: Fly the 180° in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Downwind at pattern altitude, before-landing checklist complete
Abreast of the spot: close the throttle and hold altitude
At glide speed or 1.4 VSO: lower the nose and trim
Shape the base leg for wind and height; initial flaps if needed
Turn final onto the centerline; flaps as needed, 1.3 VSO
Full flaps only once the spot is assured
Round out and touch down in the landing attitude

activities.title: Glide and landing math
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your main tires hold 30 psi. Using the AFH formula, at about what speed can dynamic hydroplaning start on a wet runway?
items.why: Minimum dynamic hydroplaning speed is 8.6 times the square root of tire pressure: 8.6 x sqrt(30) = 8.6 x 5.48 = 47.1, about 47 knots [[24:208|AFH 9-37]].

items.q: VSO is 50 knots and the POH lists no glide speed. What speed do you hold after closing the throttle at the key?
Same airplane (VSO 50 knots). What final approach speed do you set once flaps are out?
items.why: On final, establish 1.3 VSO: 1.3 x 50 = 65 knots [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

items.q: You finish your slip late and cross the threshold at 90 feet instead of 50. About how much landing distance does that add?
items.why: Each 10 feet above 50 feet adds about 200 feet: (90 - 50) / 10 = 4, and 4 x 200 = 800 feet [[27:34|AC 91-79B 5.2.3]].

items.q: The examiner's point is 1,000 feet past the threshold. What is the farthest touchdown from the threshold that still meets the ACS?
items.why: The ACS allows touchdown on the point or within 200 feet beyond it: 1,000 + 200 = 1,200 feet (ACS CA.IV.M.S8). Landing short of 1,000 feet fails [[24:195|AFH 9-24]].

activities.title: Power-off 180 with a twist
activities.intro: You are flying N52RT, a fixed-gear trainer, on your commercial checkride. The examiner wants a power-off 180° to the 1,000-foot markers on runway 18. Wind is 160° at 12 knots. You are on a right downwind at 1,000 feet AGL.

steps.s: You come abreast of the 1,000-foot markers.
options: Fly 10 more seconds, then close it
Close the throttle now
Close it once you are abeam the runway numbers
Wait and close it in the turn to base
steps.why: The downwind key is where you are abreast of the spot: close the throttle there and hold altitude while slowing to glide speed or 1.4 VSO [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]. Flying on past the spot is the overextended-downwind error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

steps.s: Halfway through the turn to base, the spot looks farther away than usual for your height. You will be low.
options: Add a little power to make up for the lost height and recover the glide
Pull the nose up to stretch the glide so that you reach the spot sooner
Shorten the base: dog-leg toward the runway and hold off flaps
Lower full flaps to steepen the glide and make the turn to final sooner
steps.why: Low means too little energy (application). The AFH lets you dog-leg toward the runway on base and use late flaps [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. Power and stretching are not options [[24:198|AFH 9-27]] [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

steps.s: Your fix works too well. You roll out on final high and on speed, with partial flaps.
options: Dive at the spot to get down, then level off before the flare
Retract the flaps to slow down and settle onto the spot
Add flaps as needed, or slip briefly into the wind
Hold it and plan to force it on at the spot with a firm touchdown
steps.why: High on final: lower flaps as required or use a forward slip briefly to steepen without gaining speed [[24:201|AFH 9-30]] [[24:197|AFH 9-26]]. Diving builds a high sink rate [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

steps.s: Which wing do you lower for the slip?
options: The left wing
The right wing
Either, it doesn't matter
Neither; crab instead
steps.why: Wind from 160° on runway 18 comes from the left. Lower the upwind (left) wing to slip into the wind [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

steps.s: At 100 feet, a gust drops your airspeed 10 knots and the spot starts moving up the windshield. You will land short.
options: Pull back to reach the spot, even at the cost of airspeed
Skid the airplane toward the spot using rudder
Raise the flaps to float farther and land on the runway
Go around: full power, attitude, then flaps
steps.why: Never stretch the glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. A sudden airspeed loss may be wind shear [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Go around: power, attitude, configuration [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Safety comes before the Task (ACS Appendix 3).

final_quiz.q: You reach the downwind key 15 knots faster than glide speed and close the throttle. What do you do first?
options: Hold altitude until speed decays to glide speed, then lower the nose and trim
Lower the nose right away to start down and let the speed bleed off in the descent
Lower full flaps at once to slow down and save altitude before the base turn
Add some power back to keep the speed up and stay on the planned path
final_quiz.why: When abreast of the spot, close the throttle and hold altitude while slowing to the recommended glide speed or 1.4 VSO [[24:198|AFH 9-27]]. Then set pitch for that speed and trim [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Early flaps are a common error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

final_quiz.q: Your trainer has a 9 to 1 glide ratio. In still air at best glide, about how far can you glide from 800 feet AGL?
options: About 900 feet
About 9,800 feet
About 7,200 feet
About 3,600 feet
final_quiz.why: Glide ratio is distance traveled per altitude lost: 800 x 9 = 7,200 feet [[24:82|AFH 3-21]].

final_quiz.q: On base you need a 15° crab to hold your track, much more than usual. How does that help your plan?
options: It means you should turn final early regardless of height, since the wind is strong
It only matters on final, not on base, because wind drift is judged at the runway
It means the airspeed indicator is wrong, since a crab angle shouldn't be needed
It shows the wind is strong, which helps plan the turn to final and flap timing
final_quiz.why: The amount of crab needed on base shows the wind's strength and direction. That helps plan the turn to final and gives some indication of when to lower flaps [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

final_quiz.q: Today you are 300 pounds lighter than last week, same wind. Flown at the correct glide speed for each weight, how does your glide distance compare?
options: Shorter, because lighter airplanes sink faster
The same distance, but it takes longer
It depends only on flap setting
Longer, because a lighter airplane always glides farther
final_quiz.why: Weight does not affect glide angle at the proper speed. Both cover the same distance; the lighter airplane just takes longer [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

final_quiz.q: On final you are high and on glide speed, with only partial flaps out. Using the energy matrix, which box are you in, and what is the right fix?
options: Box 8, total energy high: dive at the spot to lose the excess height
Box 1, total energy OK: just lower the nose and hold the glide speed
Box 4, total energy high: add drag with more flaps or a brief slip
Box 5, desired state: change nothing and hold the present flaps and speed
final_quiz.why: Higher at the desired airspeed is box 4, a total energy error [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]. Normally the throttle fixes that, but it stays closed here. When high on final, the AFH says to lower flaps as required or use a forward slip, which steepens the path without adding speed [[24:201|AFH 9-30]] [[24:197|AFH 9-26]].

final_quiz.q: You are faster than best glide on final and slightly high. What does lowering the nose do?
options: Reduces airspeed and steepens the descent
Has no effect on the descent angle
Increases airspeed and shallows the descent
Increases airspeed and steepens the descent
final_quiz.why: Above best glide, pitching down increases the airspeed and steepens the descent angle [[24:195|AFH 9-24]]. That extra speed can then cause floating past the spot [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].

final_quiz.q: On every practice lap you aim for the same farmhouse as your base key. Why does the AFH warn against this?
options: Farmhouses are noise-sensitive areas, and flying over them repeatedly annoys the owners
The base key must always be at exactly 500 feet AGL, never at a ground point
Ground references are not allowed during a checkride, so they teach bad habits
If the landmark isn't there, you are lost; vary altitude and location instead
final_quiz.why: The base key is not a fixed point on the ground. Tying it to a landmark leaves you at a loss when the object isn't there, so vary altitude and location in practice [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

final_quiz.q: Your examiner's point is the runway numbers. Why might you suggest a point farther down the runway on your own practice flights?
options: The numbers give no safety cushion for a mechanical problem or misjudgment
The ACS requires a point at least 500 feet down the runway on every power-off landing
It lets you use power on short final to reach the spot more easily
It makes the maneuver easier to fail, so you only try it with an instructor
final_quiz.why: Selecting the runway numbers as the touchdown point gives no safety cushion; a point farther down adds margin [[24:196|AFH 9-25]].

final_quiz.q: On your checkride a vehicle enters the runway and you go around from short final. How does the ACS treat that go-around for this Task?
options: Unsatisfactory, because any go-around on the checkride fails this Task automatically
Satisfactory only if your next touchdown is within 400 feet beyond the point
Not unsatisfactory, because it was a runway safety concern beyond your control
The examiner must end the checkride because the Task cannot be completed
final_quiz.why: ACS Appendix 3: a go-around because you can't meet the skill tolerances is unsatisfactory, but a go-around for runway safety concerns beyond the applicant's or evaluator's control is not. Neither of you may force a landing to finish the Task. AFH says any approach may end in a go-around, and the danger is delaying it, not the go-around itself [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

final_quiz.q: You touch down 150 feet past the point, on centerline, in a slight right drift. Is that within ACS standards?
options: Yes, it is inside 200 feet, so the drift is minor
No, because the ACS requires no side drift at touchdown
No, because any touchdown past the point fails the Task
Yes, drift only matters in tailwheel airplanes
final_quiz.why: The standard is on or within 200 feet beyond the point, with no side drift and the longitudinal axis aligned with and over the centerline (ACS CA.IV.M.S8). Drift side-loads the gear [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

final_quiz.q: Low on base, you feel the urge to add bottom rudder to tighten the turn to final while holding back pressure. What is the danger?
options: A slip that will make you land long and leave too little runway to stop
A cross-control stall that can quickly become a spin
Carburetor ice from the low power setting during the extended glide
Overspeeding the flaps because the steeper bank adds airspeed on final
final_quiz.why: Excess rudder with opposite aileron and back pressure in a power-off approach can become a cross-control condition; a stall there almost certainly brings a rapid spin [[24:85|AFH 3-24]]. Skidding turns are a listed common error [[24:198|AFH 9-27]].

final_quiz.q: You are flying a power-off 180° into a 20-knot headwind on final and sinking toward the near edge of your aiming area. Which technique does the AFH list for this?
options: Adding power on short final
Raising flaps to reduce drag
Pulling the nose up to stretch the glide
Flying slightly above best glide in the headwind
final_quiz.why: The AFH lists increasing airspeed slightly above best glide in a headwind as a way to stabilize the rest of the approach [[24:196|AFH 9-25]]. A headwind shortens the glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]].

final_quiz.q: Tower offers you LAHSO for your power-off 180°. The hold-short point leaves little room past your spot. What should you do?
options: Decline it; the PIC may refuse any LAHSO clearance that would compromise safety
Accept; LAHSO is mandatory once offered, and declining is a violation of the clearance
Accept and plan a firm touchdown short of the point, using full flaps and brakes
Accept but ignore the hold-short line if you float, since a go-around costs time
final_quiz.why: The PIC has final authority to accept or decline LAHSO and is expected to decline if it would compromise safety; know the ALD first [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]].
